Bringing your dog to Japan from Finland

Japan doesn’t count Finland as one of its designated rabies-free regions, so the full process applies: an ISO microchip, two rabies vaccinations, a rabies antibody test (FAVN) at a Japan-designated laboratory, and a wait of at least 180 days after the blood draw before your dog arrives.

These are all the steps for a dog starting from scratch. If your dog is already microchipped or vaccinated, some are already done: build your personalized checklist to see exactly what’s left, with dates.

Build my checklist

📋

Foundations

The identity and vaccination chain everything else depends on.

1

Implant an ISO-compliant microchip (if not already done)

Your dog needs an ISO 11784/11785-compliant 15-digit microchip, and it must be implanted BEFORE any rabies vaccination that will count toward Japan's requirements — vaccinations given before the chip generally don't count (MAFF accepts them only under narrow conditions, so ask AQS if this applies to you). The chip and the first vaccination can happen on the same visit, chip first. Note: microchips starting with the prefix ‘900 202’ are currently rejected by Japan. MAFF has also warned (December 2025) that some chips starting with ‘900’ have been found with the same number implanted in different animals, which can mean re-chipping and redoing the process — if your chip starts with 900, check with AQS early.
2

Confirm your microchip number is recorded on every document

The exact same 15-digit microchip number needs to appear, digit-for-digit, on every document — the vaccination certificates, any antibody test report, and the government-endorsed health certificate (Form AC, or Form AB for designated regions). Mismatches between documents are one of the most common reasons paperwork gets rejected or delayed — it's worth triple-checking this yourself rather than assuming it's automatically consistent.
3

Complete two rabies vaccinations, at least 30 days apart

For non-designated-region dogs, Japan requires two or more rabies vaccinations. The first must be given after the microchip is implanted, and your dog must be at least 91 days old. The second dose must be given at least 30 days after the first, and while the first dose's immunity period is still active. Use an inactivated (killed) or recombinant vaccine — live and RNA vaccines are not accepted.
4

Confirm the vaccine is inactivated (killed) or recombinant — not live or RNA

Japan only accepts inactivated (killed virus) or recombinant rabies vaccines — not modified-live or RNA vaccines. The certificate must show the product name and manufacturer, so check yours or ask your vet to confirm.
🧪

Antibody Testing & Timing

The part with the hard deadlines.

5

Get a FAVN (or RFFIT) antibody titer test at a Japan-designated laboratory

The blood draw must happen after the second rabies vaccination (the same day is fine), after the microchip was implanted, and while the vaccination is still within its immunity period. It must be sent to a laboratory Japan specifically designates for this test — not just any vet lab. The required result is a titer of 0.5 IU/mL or higher; if it comes back lower, your dog has to be retested, and the 180-day wait runs from the passing test's blood draw. Ask your vet which designated lab they use, or check MAFF's current list.
6

Wait out the 180-day clock from your blood draw

You cannot bring your dog into Japan until at least 180 days have passed since the FAVN blood draw (day of the draw counts as day 0). There's no way to expedite this — a dog that arrives early is held in quarantine at the airport for the shortfall — so it's worth building your whole timeline backward from this date.
7

Know your FAVN's 2-year outer validity — and don't let vaccine coverage lapse

Your FAVN result is valid for 2 years from the blood draw date — but only as long as your dog's rabies vaccine coverage never lapses in the meantime. If a booster is missed and coverage lapses even briefly, the whole process resets: new vaccinations, a brand-new FAVN test, and a fresh 180-day wait from scratch. As long as each booster is given before the prior one's labeled immunity period runs out, your original FAVN stays valid for the full 2 years — and if you arrive later than that, a second antibody test covers you without another 180-day wait (see the next item).
📄

Paperwork & Government Sign-off

The forms and endorsements Japan actually requires.

8

Use Japan's recommended certificate, Form AC (or your country's Japan-specific equivalent)

Japan requires a health certificate issued or endorsed by your country's government that contains a specific list of items: your dog's ID and microchip, your (the traveler's) and the receiving contact's details in Japan, full vaccination history, the antibody test result, and a clinical exam confirmation. MAFF strongly recommends using its own form, Form AC, so nothing is missed. A generic export certificate is only acceptable if it contains every required item — usually it doesn't. A few countries have a Japan-specific certificate that replaces Form AC (for example the UK's EHC 6407 and Spain's ASE-3293); check your country's note below.

📍 Specific to Finland: In Finland, an official certificate is always issued by a municipal or city veterinarian (kunnaneläinlääkäri) — for Japan, they sign Japan's Form AC as the official vet. Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority) has a Japan page that refers to Japan's own requirements.
9

Get your certificate endorsed by your country's official government veterinary authority

After your treating vet completes and signs the certificate (Form AC, or Form AB for designated regions), it must be endorsed by your country's official government veterinary authority (for example, CFIA in Canada, APHIS in the United States, or your national equivalent) — usually for a fee, and often needing to be booked in advance. Japan requires the original endorsed certificate (some countries' electronic certificates are also accepted).

📍 Specific to Finland: Book your municipal or city veterinarian. Ruokavirasto gives advice (vienti.lemmikit@ruokavirasto.fi) and can confirm the official vet's authority afterwards if Japan asks.
10

Submit advance notification to Japan's Animal Quarantine Service — at least 40 days before arrival

This is one of the most commonly missed steps because it happens well before travel and isn't part of the vet paperwork. You (or your agent) must notify the Animal Quarantine Service office at your expected Japanese port of entry at least 40 days before your dog's arrival — online through NACCS (MAFF's preferred method), or by email if you can't use NACCS. Notifications made less than 40 days ahead are, in principle, not accepted. Do this even if your other paperwork isn't finalized yet — it's based on your planned itinerary. Dogs can only enter through certain designated airports and seaports, so check your port is one of them. Once approved, AQS sends an 'Approval of Import Inspection', which some airlines ask to see.
11

Book the pre-export clinical exam — within 10 days of departure

A vet (or official government vet) must examine your dog within 10 days before boarding, confirming the microchip reads correctly and there are no clinical signs of rabies (or leptospirosis, for dogs). This exam result gets recorded on Form AC, so it needs to happen close to your actual travel date, not earlier.
✈️

Travel Logistics

Crates, airlines, and getting there.

12

Book an IATA-compliant crate and confirm your airline's pet policy

Make sure your crate meets IATA Live Animals Regulations sizing (your dog should be able to stand, turn around, and lie down naturally). Confirm with your airline: cabin vs. cargo eligibility, any breed restrictions (many airlines restrict flat-faced breeds from cargo), temperature embargo policies, and whether they require a direct/nonstop routing.
13

Travel with original documents, not photocopies

Bring the original government-endorsed health certificate (Form AC, or Form AB for designated regions) and, if you had one, the original antibody test report from the lab — not copies. Bring your vaccination certificates too. Keep everything together in a single folder you can access quickly at check-in and on arrival. (Japan accepts electronic certificates from a few countries, including the US, Brazil and Spain.)
🇯🇵

Arrival in Japan

What happens when you land.

14

Present your dog and documents at Animal Quarantine on arrival

On arrival in Japan, you'll go through the Animal Quarantine Service counter before regular customs. If your advance notification was filed correctly and your documents are complete and consistent, inspection is typically quick. If documents are missing, inconsistent, or requirements weren't met, your dog can be held in quarantine for up to 180 days — which is exactly why getting the paperwork right in advance matters so much.
🔄

Returning Home

A separate process from getting into Japan — plan the trip home too.

15

Apply for Japan's own export inspection — at least 14 days before departure

Leaving Japan with your dog is its own separate process, run by the same Animal Quarantine Service (AQS) that handled your arrival — it does not happen automatically just because you're leaving. Apply for export inspection through NACCS, or by email to your local AQS office, at least 14 days before your desired inspection date, attaching your dog's veterinary certificates. The actual inspection happens within 10 days of departure, and AQS issues an English-language export certificate on the spot if everything checks out. If someone other than you brings the dog to the inspection, they'll need a Power of Attorney document from you.
16

Check what your home country requires to bring your dog back from Japan

This is governed entirely by your OWN country's pet import rules, not Japan's — it's a completely separate process from everything else on this checklist. The good news: most countries classify Japan as low-risk for rabies, so returning is often (not always) simpler than the outbound trip was. Confirm directly with your country's own import authority well before you travel — don't assume it mirrors the outbound process.

📍 Specific to Finland: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Finland on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. Finland also requires anti-Echinococcus tapeworm treatment 24-120 hours before arrival, documented on the certificate or passport. Customs checks your dog at Helsinki-Vantaa.
